product: Four Seasons blower motor, motor only
meets: Listed for 1979-83 and 1985 RX-7; the interchange list carries Mazda 8871-76-453 (the OE number). 12 V, 2 wires, flanged, 3.0 in dia x 3.875 in, shaft 0.268 in x 2.06 in
why: The only current aftermarket motor that lists FB fitment; 2-wire as L3-BLW wants; cheap and in stock
drawbacks: It ships WITHOUT the fan wheel. The record assumed the squirrel cage transfers, but the factory motor is gone, and no aftermarket wheel for the FB turned up. The wheel must come from the old assembly or be found used. Its current draw is published nowhere; the record plans 12-18 A on high, a forum estimate says about 5 A. Do not buy 35677, which is the 1984-85 part
confirm: That the original fan wheel still exists and its bore fits the 0.268 in shaft; the real amps on high, measured (then LD09 and the O16 limit are set from it)
said: i still have to old one with the fanwheel, rock auto is perfect

product: Genuine Mazda blower motor with its wheel, used or new old stock
meets: The factory part, with the correct wheel
why: Guaranteed to fit the heater box and brings the wheel - solves the missing-wheel problem
drawbacks: A 40-year-old motor: worn brushes and bearings, no warranty; supply is sporadic and the price is unknown

product: Pololu G2 High-Power Motor Driver 24v21
meets: PWM to 100 kHz (run it at 25-40 kHz, above hearing); inputs take 1.8, 3.3 and 5 V logic, so the Teensy drives it directly; 6.5-40 V (40 V absolute max); short-circuit, reverse-voltage and undervoltage protection; current-sense output 0.02 V/A; 1.3 x 0.8 in, fits the resistor-pack hole
why: Silence was the whole point of the >= 20 kHz stage (D-257), and this is the one that is truly silent. It also has the most voltage headroom, and its current sense lets the DCU spot a seized motor. Pololu is a reputable maker
drawbacks: Rated 21 A continuous without a heat sink - BELOW the record spec of >= 25 A. It is fine if the blower draws what it probably draws (5-18 A in its own airflow), but it does not meet the letter of the spec, so accepting it widens LP18 to 21 A. It is an H-bridge board, not a low-side switch: the motor goes across its two outputs, and a Schottky across the motor is still worth adding. Bare board, not automotive-rated, no over-temperature cutoff; conformal-coat it
confirm: The motor's real amps (PK001) - under about 15 A this is clearly right; board mounting in the airflow
recommend: (a), unless you want the letter of the 25 A spec over silence - then veto it and the held Cytron (30 A, but at 20 kHz a faint whine is possible) goes up next.
said: a i will monitor battery life when blasting for hours, (worth noting in enine swap that alternator needs to be beefy)

product: Cytron MD30C R2 30 A DC motor driver
meets: 30 A continuous, 80 A for 1 s; 3.3 V and 5 V logic; PWM up to 20 kHz; 5-30 V
why: Meets the >= 25 A letter of the spec with margin, inside budget
drawbacks: 20 kHz is its ceiling, right at the edge of hearing, so a faint whine is possible - the thing D-257 exists to avoid. The 30 V maximum is thin for a car and needs a TVS on its input. Bare board, no over-temperature shutdown
confirm: A whine test on the bench; board size against the resistor hole

product: FEETECH FS5115M high-torque analog servo
meets: All-metal gears, two ball bearings, 15.5 kg-cm at 6 V; 500-2500 us pulse, about 180 degrees; Pololu states it runs on 3.3 V and 5 V signals, so the DCU's 3.3 V through 330 ohm is fine
why: Plenty of torque for cable-pulled doors, metal gears, a reputable seller that documents 3.3 V compatibility, and analog, so it does not hunt and chatter against cable preload the way a digital servo does
drawbacks: Four cost about $128, just over the $60-120 budget (5+ are $30.14 each). Stall current is over 3 A at 6 V, above the 1-2.5 A the DCU rail assumed; the 5 A rail still covers one servo moving at a time (F-017 already sequences them). Pololu warns that stalling or back-driving damages it, so the firmware must stop short of the door stops. No temperature rating is published (hobby servos are usually 60 C) and it is not sealed
confirm: Behind-dash temperature in summer; set endpoints at commissioning so it never stalls
said: yes worth the extra for better servos

product: DSSERVO DS3218MG 20 kg digital servo, 180-degree version
meets: 19-21.5 kg-cm, metal gears, aluminium middle case, listed IP66; 4.8-6.8 V
why: Cheap enough to buy spares, and sealed against condensation and dust
drawbacks: A clone-market part with variable quality; stall current, temperature rating and 3.3 V signal acceptance are unpublished. Being digital it holds position with current and may buzz against cable preload unless pulses stop after each move
confirm: Bench-test one on 3.3 V through 330 ohm first

product: Blue Sea Systems ST Blade Fuse Block, 6 circuits, with cover
meets: 6 bussed positions, 30 A per circuit, 100 A per block, 32 V DC; ATO/ATC fuses; clear latched cover with 2 spare-fuse slots and labels; #10-32 input stud
why: Exactly the block LP21 describes: six bussed positions and a cover, with about 4x headroom over the ~25 A it will carry; no negative bus, which is not needed
drawbacks: The #10-32 input stud needs the right ring terminal on the O15 feed; the footprint is unconfirmed but should be a little under the 5025's 3.3 x 4.9 in
confirm: Price (probably $28-40) and that it fits behind the centre stack
said: follow recommendations, i will make space work

product: Blue Sea Systems ST Blade Fuse Block, 6 circuits, negative bus and cover
meets: Same ratings as the 5028 plus a ground bus; 3.32 x 4.9 x 1.52 in
why: Same quality, price confirmed
drawbacks: The ground bus it adds is not needed and makes it bigger

product: Universal 2-seat carbon-fibre seat heater kit, 4 pads (pads only are used)
meets: Four pads, 480 x 280 x 5 mm, 27 W +/- 3 W each, so two pads per seat is about 5.1 A at 13.5 V (5.6 A at the top of tolerance): under the 7.5 A fuse and the BTS3011TE's 10 A. A thermostat on each pad, 65 C (+10/-5)
why: The only candidate whose listing states a thermostat and its trip temperature - the heater is a safety load and must have its own cutoff. Within budget for both seats
drawbacks: Unbranded, and quality varies by seller. Listings for the same kit say the pads cannot be cut, and heater pads block air: on a seat that is also ventilated (LP31) the pads have to sit around the vent area. Not yet confirmed that the thermostat is in series inside each pad rather than in the kit's harness, which is thrown away - if it is in the harness, the protection is lost
confirm: Thermostat is inline on the pad's own leads (a meter across a pad, cold and hot); the FB cushion and back insert are at least 280 mm wide; pad and vent layout on the same seat
said: no for now, i want to first look for seats with heating/cooling and likely electric controls

product: Rostra universal carbon-fibre seat heater, one per seat
meets: 267 x 483 mm pads; temperature sensors on the bottom and back pads with continuous overheat monitoring
why: An established US maker of aftermarket seat heaters, with protection designed in on both pads
drawbacks: About twice the budget ($172 for two seats). Pad current is not published, and it is not confirmed whether its sensors are series thermostats or feed a control box in the harness - if they feed a control, discarding the harness loses the protection. The pads cannot be trimmed

product: Build: Delta centrifugal blowers, 2 per seat, over a 3D spacer-mesh layer under the cover
maker_pn: Delta BFB0712HH-A (x4) + 10 mm polyester spacer mesh, about 1 square metre
meets: Each blower 76 x 76 x 25 mm, 12 V, 0.34 A, 15.3 CFM - two per seat is about 0.7 A, far under the 2.5 A design and 5 A fuse; brushless, so PWM or reduced voltage slows it
why: No reputable seat-ventilation kit exists at this budget - the branded one (LeatherSeats SANCTUM) is $350 a seat and a Peltier unit far over the 2.5 A. This build uses datasheet-grade parts with a known current, about $70-90 all in
drawbacks: You design the ducting: pockets cut in the foam for the blowers, channels up to the mesh. 51 dBA at full speed, so it runs at a reduced duty. 25 mm deep, which has to fit under the FB cushion. The FB's cloth covers pass air; leather would need perforating
confirm: Depth available under the seat pan; the blower location; mesh price
said: no for now, i want to first look for seats with heating/cooling and likely electric controls

product: Grote LED sealed-beam headlamp, 4x6, high and low beam in one unit

product: Song Chuan 871 micro ISO relay, SPDT, 12 V, coil diode
meets: Standard micro ISO blades (fits the Waytek 75290 sockets the electrical build fits - an "ISO 280" relay would not); NO 35 A / NC 20 A at 14 V; 1N4007 across the coil with its anode on 85, so 86 is positive - which is how K3/K4 are wired (86 on the O10 release branch, 85 switched low by the DCU)
why: The same family as the electrical build's own relays (P003), with the diode the DCU's low-side switch needs, in the right polarity
drawbacks: Flux-tight, not sealed - fine behind the dash

product: TE Micro Relay A, SPDT, 12 V, coil diode
meets: Micro ISO, IP54; NO 30 A / NC 20 A at 23 C
why: A top-tier maker, sealed to IP54
drawbacks: Price unconfirmed; which printed terminal carries 86 must be checked against the diode drawing

product: Song Chuan 871 micro ISO relay, SPDT, 12 V, coil resistor (x4) - plus two blade fuses for F8 / F9
meets: Fits the sill sockets; NO 35 A makes and breaks the window feed, NC 20 A carries the motor's ground return and the braking short; 680 ohm coil resistor, no polarity to get wrong; -40 to 125 C
why: The same family as every other relay in the car. A resistor, not a diode, because a coil diode slows the release and shortens contact life when breaking motor current (both TE and Song Chuan warn of this)
drawbacks: The NC contact's 20 A resistive rating is marginal against a window motor's 15-20 A stall - the window motors (LP36) are not chosen yet, so this is confirmed when they are
confirm: Window motor stall current against 20 A NC (LP36)

product: TE Micro Relay A, SPDT, 12 V, coil resistor (x4)
